newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rack up second straight day of gains.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rack up second straight day of gains.

text.p: Stocks racked up gains for a second consecutive session Wednesday as investors rushed back into the market to buy the biggest names in technology before year-end.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 38.44 points at 6,346.77, adding to Tuesday's rally of nearly 40 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,572 to 927 on active volume of 500 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
International Business Machines Corp. led the blue chips, surging 6-7/8 to 158-3/4, contributing more than half the Dow index's advance.
"Stocks are in a year-end window-dressing rally and IBM is the one all the money managers want in their portfolios," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
The technology-laced Nasdaq Composite index jumped 19.06 points to 1,285.38.
Analysts said the market was showing some early signs of the so-called Santa Claus rally, the late December advance that stocks enjoy nearly every year.
"My suspicion is that we're looking at the early part of it," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "This is a classic time of year when the market has an upside bias."

The rally broadened considerably over Tuesday, but analysts reckoned that a sustained rise was unlikely until the market steers clear of the late-year portfolio shifting by money managers and the spectre of Friday's triple-witching expiration of futures, index options and stock options.
"Is this the start of a new breakout? Probably not," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co.

"I wouldn't read too much into it because it's hard to distinguish what's going on in the last days of a year and it's an options expirations week," he said. "Plus, interest rates are still high and that's a challenge for stocks."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond lost 16/32, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, to 6.70 percent from 6.66 percent at Tuesday's close.
"This can't go on forever," said Barthel. "There's a very good correlation that says when interest rates go up, the market pays the penalty."
For investors in technology shares, the upturn in interest rates seemed little more than a footnote, however.
Intel Corp. jumped 5-3/4 to 135-3/4 and Microsoft Corp. climbed 2-3/4 to 82-5/8.
Compaq Computer Corp. raced higher, adding 6-1/2 to 78-3/4 after SoundView Financial raised its near-term rating on the shares.
Drug companies' stocks also gained, with Pfizer Inc. up 5/8 to 81-3/8 and Johnson & Johnson up 1/2 to 49-1/8.
Warner-Lambert Co. rose 3/8 to 74-5/8 after the company said it won Food and Drug Administration approval to sell its new cholesterol-cutting drug Lipitor.
Merck & Co. Inc. gained 5/8 to 76-7/8. It said its fourth quarter and 1997 earnings would be on the high end of Wall Street's estimates.

Genetics Institute Inc. soared 22-3/4 to 84-1/2 after American Home Products Corp. said it would buy the 40 percent of Genetics Institute it does not already own for $85 a share. American Home Products fell 1/8 to 59-1/8.

ADT Ltd. rose 3-1/8 to 23-1/4 after Western Resources Inc. extended an unsolicited $3.5 billion offer to buy the company. Analysts called the bid, which values ADT at 22-1/2 per share, a low-ball offer that was likely to be raised.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 5.50 points to 731.54. The American Stock Exchange index rose 4.65 to 574.96.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 2.40 to 385.17. The average share was up 25 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,083.246 up 55.116 or 0.78 percent.
